doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

title: Silent movie accompaniment and Eugene Ormandy
summary: His mother played for silent films in Birmingham; Henderson recalls Ormandy's remarks on theatre orchestra music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I understand that you played some for silent movies too, or of making them not silent, in the movie houses.

Yeah. Well my mother did that, that’s where I started. She was a church organist in Birmingham, England, and then at night, a couple of nights a week, I believe it was Friday and Saturday, she used to go to the local cinema house and play an old beat up upright piano, and watch the screen. That fascinated me because I was already very — she had the hammer on me to study, and I went down to the London Conservatory when I was very young. I stayed away from home as we say.
On those movies, did they give you a score of musical cues?
But it was partly up to you?

It was really, you know when Ormandy — God rest his soul — when Eugene Ormandy was alive, he and I used to talk a lot about that, because he conducted at the Capitol Theater in New York, and he once mentioned something to me how he said, in Hungarian he wouldn’t say tampered, he acquired melodic content that didn’t belong in the film. And he said what the things that they sent for the theater orchestras to play, an orangutan could conduct. You know he said there was no interest in the music. So he began really to investigate music structure in the classical school even though he had had the schooling as a player. And he said that really was the motivation for his conducting career. Isn’t that amazing? The years before the Philadelphia Orchestra. He was a wonderful man. He was strange, warm. For ten years he said, “You conduct my orchestra” but I never did. When he passed away I was invited to conduct his orchestra. So typical of our profession.
